title: IC 4499: A globular cluster’s age revisited
caption: The globular cluster IC 4499, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: IC 4499 · constellation Apus · about 55000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Hubble captures IC 4499, one of the large, ball-shaped groups of old stars called globular clusters that circle a galaxy. It has long been thought that all the stars in one form at about the same time, a property that can be used to work out a cluster's age.

For heavier globulars, careful observations tell a different story, since they appear to hold several populations of stars born at different times. Gravity is thought to be one reason. IC 4499 is a useful in-between case, with a mass between the simple low-mass clusters and the more complex massive ones. Astronomers found no sign of multiple generations in it, supporting the idea that less massive clusters generally host just one.

Hubble has also helped pin down the cluster's age. Observations from the 1990s suggested it was puzzlingly young compared with other Milky Way globulars, but newer Hubble data make it much more likely that IC 4499 is roughly as old as the others, at about 12 billion years.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.41 x 3.49 arcminutes) and distance (55000 light years), the frame spans roughly 55 × 56 light-years. Its light set out about 55,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared exposures from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble's sharp view separates stars in a distant cluster.
